title: Two kinds of sensation
objective: Contrast somatic and visceral sensation in quality and localization.

steps.title: Sharp and placed vs dull and vague
steps.body: **Somatic** sensation from the skin is usually sharp and well-localized (deep muscle and joint pain is duller). **Visceral** sensation (gut, pancreas, bladder) is typically dull, aching, and hard to place. The difference comes largely from how densely each is innervated.

steps.prompt: Match each sensation to its usual character.
steps.explanation: Dense skin innervation gives precise somatic sensation; sparse visceral innervation gives vague, diffuse sensation.

steps.prompt: Why can't you pinpoint a stomachache the way you locate a pinprick on your hand?
options: Viscera are sparsely innervated, with large receptive fields
Gut afferents conduct too slowly to carry location
Visceral pain travels only in the vagus, not the cord
The brain ignores gut signals unless they are severe
steps.explanation: Few afferents with big [[receptive field|receptive fields]] can't give the brain a fine spatial map, so visceral sensation is diffuse.

variants.setup: You compare locating a pinprick on skin vs an ache in the gut.
variants.reveal: Dense skin innervation pinpoints the pinprick; sparse gut innervation can't localize the ache.

steps.title: Different jobs
steps.body: Skin needs a fine map to guide action. Viscera mostly need to flag *that* something is wrong — over-stretch, inflammation, ischemia — so their afferents are tuned to those events, not to precise location.

reviewNotes: Somatic vs visceral sensation; sets up referred pain.
